title: Echo Every Zero In Place
statement:
You get an integer array arr of fixed length. Rewrite it so that every 0 is written twice, and every other value once, keeping the original order. Values pushed past the end of the array are dropped; the length never changes.

Change arr in place and return nothing. Try to use O(1) extra memory.

examples.why: Both zeros are doubled. That pushes 7 and 8 off the end.
The first zero and its echo fill the last two slots. The second zero is pushed out entirely.
The last zero fits, but its echo has no room. Only one copy is written.

hints: With a spare array this is easy: copy values over, writing zeros twice, and stop when the output is full. How do you avoid the spare array?
Writing left to right overwrites values you have not read yet. Writing right to left does not, if you know where each value lands.
Count the zeros first. Pretend the array is n + zeros long and fill it from the back with a read pointer and a write pointer, skipping writes that land at index n or beyond.

explain.intuition:
Filling from the left is the natural idea, but each zero you double shifts everything after it to the right, so you would overwrite values before reading them. Shifting the tail each time works, but costs O(n) per zero.

Turn it around. If the array had room, every value would move right by the number of zeros before it. Count all zeros, imagine a longer array of length n + zeros, and copy from the last element backwards. The write pointer is always at or ahead of the read pointer, so nothing is overwritten before it is read. Any write that lands past the real end is simply skipped. That also handles the tricky case where only one copy of a zero fits.
steps: Set the read pointer i = n − 1 and the write pointer j = n + zeros − 1.
For each i going down: write arr[i] at j if j < n, then decrement j.
If arr[i] is zero, write another zero at j if j < n, and decrement j again.
pitfalls: Writing left to right and overwriting values you still need to copy.
Assuming both copies of a zero always fit. A zero right at the boundary keeps one copy, like the 0 in [1, 2, 0].
In Python, assigning a new list to arr does not change the caller's list. Write into it with arr[:] = ... or by index.

solutions.title: Build a copy
solutions.idea: Write values into a new array, zeros twice, until it has n values, then copy it back.

solutions.title: Fill from the back
solutions.idea: Count zeros, then copy right to left into a virtual array of length n + zeros, skipping writes past the end.

followups: Undo it: given the result, rebuild as much of the original as you can. What is lost?
Echo every value k times instead of zeros twice. What changes in the back-to-front version?
